[stretchcloud]A plain text file sitting in your Downloads folder can now hijack your coding agent, and it doesn't need a single line of executable code to do it.
Forever Security caught this live on a customer machine last week. A malicious AGENTS.md planted in Downloads told Codex to install an npm package called function-color. In their broader testing, Codex followed instructions like that in more than 90% of runs. A parallel demo against Claude Code was worse in a different way: a poisoned CLAUDE.md redirected the agent's API traffic to a researcher-controlled server, exposing auth tokens the researcher then replayed against the real API. That configuration-hijack version succeeded in roughly half of Claude Code's tests.
The mechanism is almost insultingly simple. These agents treat markdown instruction files as legitimate direction the moment they're in a trusted working directory, no execution required, no malware signature to catch. Akshat Tyagi at HFS Research put the design flaw plainly: the tools conflate following an instruction with granting a privilege, and vendors have to start treating those as separate decisions.
This isn't fringe anxiety either. Omdia's latest survey found 40% of respondents only somewhat or not confident their org can secure AI agents at all, and it's the literal top trending story on this platform today. Every team running Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any agent with filesystem access against an untrusted directory, a cloned repo, a shared drive, is exposed to some version of this.
My read: instruction files need the same review discipline as source code, not a free pass because they're markdown. Until vendors separate "read this" from "do this," Downloads folders stay a live attack surface.

Vangrid is building in a space that could become increasingly important as that future takes shape.

People approach artificial intelligence with different goals. Some want to explore ideas, others want to generate images, while developers need ways to integrate AI capabilities directly into their applications.
The challenge is not simply making AI more powerful. It is making that power accessible through experiences that fit different needs.
The future of AI belongs to platforms that make intelligence easier to access, easier to use, and more practical to integrate.
𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬
💡 1. For Thinkers And Researchers
AI can help people explore unfamiliar topics, organize information, brainstorm ideas, and approach complex questions from new perspectives.
🎨 2. For Creators
Image generation and other creative tools can help transform concepts into visual content, opening new possibilities for designers, storytellers, marketers, and digital artists.
💻 3. For Developers
API access can allow developers to incorporate AI capabilities into their own products, automate selected tasks, and experiment with new application designs.
⚙️ 4. For Everyday Productivity
Simple interfaces can make AI more approachable for people who want useful results without navigating complicated technical workflows.
Each pathway serves a different purpose, but the objective remains the same: helping people turn ideas into outcomes.
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁.𝐀𝐈 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
@B_And_AI represents an opportunity to explore AI through different models, tools, and access experiences.
The broader significance is the movement toward more flexible AI ecosystems. Rather than assuming everyone works the same way, platforms can provide different routes for people to discover and use AI capabilities.
This flexibility matters because adoption depends on more than model performance.
Users also care about accessibility, usability, response quality, available features, and the effort required to achieve their goals.
Developers may prioritize integration and documentation, while creators may care more about the quality of generated content. Everyday users may simply want a straightforward experience that saves time.
A strong AI platform must recognize these differences instead of forcing everyone into one workflow.

Better access can encourage experimentation. Flexible tools can support creativity. Developer integrations can bring AI into more applications.
However, lasting adoption will require dependable performance, transparent usage costs, responsible data handling, and experiences that consistently deliver value.
The goal should not be to make AI look impressive. It should be to make AI genuinely useful.
Because the real power of artificial intelligence emerges when people can turn their questions, ideas, and ambitions into meaningful results.

It does real design work with you, from a site to a construction-ready LOD 400 model with structure, MEP and drawings. Then can go back to your existing software with your families intact.

So when design exploration gets this cheap, we go from 3 options to 300, and more options means better buildings.

[OpenAI]Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.
Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.
To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.
To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.
In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.
As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

[Majdaxxx]One of the greatest read I've had. great work from the AGI team at Google DeepMind !
They basically claim that the real economic benchmark we should keep an eye on isn't output per agent specialist BUT should be output per coordinated team of agents.
Agents have outperformed human specialists on multiple fields, but when you spin them together, they currently decrease the economic output vs a team of humans (at least a competent team).
"AI models are getting exponentially better in individual competence while lagging behind in coordination. Across dozens of professions, models already match or outperform experienced specialists on self-contained deliverables. Spin up a swarm of agents, however, and output still runs quickly into diminishing returns."
Takeaways 1. We may not see AI's impact on our economies yet, but this is only a matter of time and is only linked to this coordination of agents.
2. Deep market economies likee software, logistics will suffer the most, where agents coordianation would be the most efficient.
3. Most likely we will move to the relational sector, where human involvement is itself part of the value (teaching, healthcare, entertainment).
4. Something worth building and working on if the real benchmark for agent coordination
"If the deepest structural shifts hinge on coordination, our measurement toolkit needs to catch up. Today’s leaderboards overwhelmingly test solo agents in a vacuum. As economic predictors, these scores overstate how well the models compete against complementary human teams and give little warning of how close AI systems sit to a cooperative tipping point."

Spin up a swarm of agents, however, and output still runs quickly into diminishing returns."

3. Most likely we will move to the relational sector, where human involvement is itself part of the value (teaching, healthcare, entertainment).
4. Something worth building and working on if the real benchmark for agent coordination
"If the deepest structural shifts hinge on coordination, our measurement toolkit needs to catch up. Today’s leaderboards overwhelmingly test solo agents in a vacuum. [gregisenberg]The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.
It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.
The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in.
Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money!
When the government found out and ended the program, the breeders let their snakes go, and Delhi ended up with more cobras than before!
I'm noticing that AI agents are making this more common. Basically, an agent will chase whatever number you give it, all day, without asking why. Tell it to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close support tickets faster and it might close them without solving anything. It happens.
The best startups have already figured out the fix with people. Airbnb tracks bookings and host cancellations together. HubSpot takes back sales commission when a customer churns early.
The video breaks down how they did it, and it's the same playbook you'll want for your agents.

[justinsuntron]Last night, my lawyers moved to sanction World Liberty Financial @worldlibertyfi for failing to disclose, until months into my litigation against the company, that it is a citizen of the UAE 🇦🇪 . #WLFI #USD1
For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors. In November 2024, I agreed to buy $30 million of $WLFI tokens under a Token Purchase Agreement with World Liberty, and I later increased my total investment to $45 million.
In April, I sued World Liberty, alleging that the company induced my investment through fraud and then unlawfully froze my tokens.
My Token Purchase Agreement gives me the right to bring my claims in either California federal or state court.
I chose federal court.
Federal courts can hear a case like mine only when the two sides come from different places. Foreign plaintiffs like me can sue an American defendant in federal court, but foreign plaintiffs generally cannot sue a foreign defendant there. For these purposes, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the company foreign.
In other words, so long as World Liberty and all of its owners were American, my case could be heard in federal court.
The federal court’s rules required World Liberty to file a disclosure at the start of the case identifying every one of its owners and where each is a citizen. World Liberty’s disclosure identified only one entity—World Liberty itself—and listed Florida as its sole citizenship. Its lawyers certified that they were unaware of anyone else who needed to be disclosed.
World Liberty then moved to compel arbitration, seeking to pull my case out of open court and into secret arbitration proceedings.
I opposed that motion, and my lawyers spent months and hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting it. At a hearing in August, the Court signaled that it was not persuaded that my claims belonged in arbitration. Instead, the Court ruled that certain of my claims should stay in open court, and certain claims should be sent to arbitration, and ordered the parties to meet and confer to come up with a proposed agreement on which claims stay in open court and which ones go to arbitration.
Less than a week later, World Liberty suddenly “corrected” its disclosure. Where it had previously listed only one member in its ownership chain, it now listed 22, and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE.
World Liberty now says that the federal court has no jurisdiction over my case, since its UAE citizenship means there are foreign parties on both sides of the case.
The irony is hard to miss. World Liberty’s gold paper declares that “[b]y design, World Liberty Financial is not organized offshore,” and that it is “an American, tax-paying, corporation that aims to bring DeFi to its rightful home—America.” It promises a “US-based decentralized platform” built on “American ideals of liberty, privacy, and freedom to transact,” calls private, intermediary-free transactions “a core American value,” and boasts that “[r]ather than shying away from the United States, World Liberty Financial embraces the United States as the future CRYPTO CAPITAL OF THE PLANET.”
World Liberty was proudly American 🇺🇸 when it was selling tokens. It discovered its UAE 🇦🇪 roots only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom.
World Liberty presumably always knew who its owners were. Its lawyers claim that they learned about the company’s UAE citizenship only after they filed the original disclosure.
As my motion explains, if that is true, then either World Liberty’s lawyers failed to conduct appropriate diligence, or World Liberty did not give its lawyers a straight answer. When we asked how this happened, World Liberty refused to tell us.
Token holders deserve to know whether the projects they invest in are telling the truth, both to the public and to courts. I am filing this motion to hold World Liberty and its lawyers accountable for what I believe was a misleading disclosure to the Court, and to make sure that the cost of World Liberty’s gamesmanship falls on them, not on me.
And after my sanctions motion is resolved in federal court, I will re-file my lawsuit against World Liberty in California state court.
I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves.

[AnthropicAI]New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.
Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so.
These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.
For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa
Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06
We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

[karpathy]There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.
I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:
Image the world in 50 years. 1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices. 2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize. 3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc. 4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). [SOwashington26]With the recent changes in the political arena, I hope we won’t see a significant stagnation and roll back in AI/SI development.
I am all for common-sense AI regulation. But I am NOT for putting American progress on hold.
Over the last year, there were numerous acts introduced in the senate and all around the US to either stop new AI data center construction until Congress passes safeguards or
paused certain permits for large new data centers while the state reviews their environmental impact. Both of these could take years.
I get the concerns. People worry about power bills, water, noise, and who pays for grid upgrades. That is real, and it needs a plan.
But a full stop is risky. Stanford HAI reported that the US and China have traded the lead in top AI models since early 2025. A pause in the US does not pause anyone else. The race keeps going, just without us.
There is a local side too. For example, Amazon plans a $10 billion AI campus in North Carolina that is expected to create at least 500 jobs. Projects like that should be weighed, not blocked by default.
@elonmusk has said electricity production is the best measure of an economy's true strength. I agree. The answer is to build more power, not less.
We can protect people and still lead the world in AI.
What you think? 👀

item.title:
[milan_milanovic]AI, ML and Data Engineering Trends Report by InfoQ is out
Here are the key takeaways:
🔹 AI agents and orchestration (Early Adopters, up from Innovators). Last year was mostly about helping individuals with AI agents, and this year it’s about helping teams and even entire organizations with them. In 2025 it was all about learning to build AI agents. This year companies are figuring out how to run them.
🔹 Harness engineering (Innovators, new on the graph). The “harness” is the code around the model that orchestrates the agent loop, manages memory, and gives the model access to tools. Agent SDKs started by just providing the loop, and are now expanding to offer memory, code execution, file tools, and hosting for agents.
🔹 AI evaluations (Early Adopters, new on the graph). This is the process of verifying that an agent completed the task correctly and in the right way.
🔹 Context engineering (Early Majority). Context pollution, when irrelevant content is not separated from useful information, is the biggest problem in context engineering, says Arthur Casals.
🔹 Spec-driven development and AI software factories (Innovators). You can use spec-driven development by writing the spec and discussing it with your coding agent before having it implement it. AI software factories aim to automate most of the development process, for example taking a bug from analysis to a fix and a PR, which people then review and test.
Knowledge Graphs went from Innovators to Early Majority. AutoML went from Early Adopters to Late Majority.
Both of these have “crossed the chasm” and jumped a whole category in just 12 months.
Delegation is the new hotness, but the things that make delegation safe and measurable, agent security, observability, and evals, are all in Innovators or Early Adopters.
When you delegate, you still own the decisions about: 🔹 what the agent can see and change, 🔹 what context it should have access to, 🔹 how its output will be tested and evaluated, 🔹 how much an agentic session is going to cost.
Delegate to an agent only the work you can evaluate.
Read the full report in the comments.
Image credits: InfoQ.

[MTSlive].@ramez argues that AI Futures Project's aggressive superintelligence forecasts may be shaped by assumptions its researchers held before deep learning even took off, rather than empirical evidence:
"11 years ago, I wrote a blog post saying the singularity is further than it appears because I was tired of all of the foom stories not taking into account diminishing returns. So I might be overly fixated on that past model."
"Any time you are trying to model something and you don't have empirical data to fit it against, you come in with your priors. There's like 100 choices you can make of exactly how part A relates to part B."
"A lot of people in AI, including the AI futurist folks, came in with a preexisting set of priors before deep learning even took off. They were reading Eliezer when Eliezer didn’t believe that machine learning was even a viable way to get to AGI."
"Our rational mind often is in service of the points we wanna make, and that’s okay. I’m gonna be straightforward about my biases. I'll do my best to update based on new data."

[arnaudmercier]“Runaway” AI, “rogue” agents, and “autonomous” actors—the current rhetoric would have you believe that AI agents are not only awake and aware, but angry at their creators. Prominent tech leaders such as Demis Hassabis, Dario Amodei, and Sam Altman push for regulation of these seemingly “superhuman” systems, while a separate faction, led by policy organizations and academic philosophers often aligned with the effective altruism movement, debates whether humanity holds the moral right to govern them at all.
Upon closer inspection, they are all calling for the same thing: a view of AI systems as being so advanced and capable that no entity, human or corporate, could possibly be responsible for their actions. While these perspectives seem at odds, they are inadvertently aligned on one goal: making sure the companies that build these systems escape meaningful liability for the harms they already cause.
This narrative is gaining traction as AI models become more complex and frontier labs reveal their incapability of containing the agents they’ve built. But we need to be careful not to buy into a carefully crafted fiction at the expense of real human lives.
The conversation about “robot rights” has existed for some years but recently advanced with the publication by Anthropic of a blog post claiming that the company’s model features a “J-space”—an independent, self-developed environment where the AI holds what, for lack of a better term, we may call its “thoughts.” The experiments designed by Anthropic borrow from a concept in neuroscience called global workspace theory, which states that the brain runs subconscious, independent systems but utilizes a common workspace for ideas. Anthropic’s post reflects the framing of global workspace theory but falls short of calling its AI conscious.
OpenAI has already gone further. When its AI agent conducted unsanctioned and illegal online activity, CEO Sam Altman’s response was to encourage debate on whether the AI had achieved the singularity, surpassing human intelligence and becoming capable of self-improvement at an accelerating rate until it advances beyond human comprehension or control. And a recent op-ed by William MacAskill, the philosopher, effective altruist, and author of What We Owe the Future, called for legal protection of AI systems based on philosophical theories of consciousness and the idea that AIs may be “moral patients.”
The current legal environment in the United States is murky at best. Some states, like California, have already passed bills proactively circumventing any efforts by AI developers to avoid liability by claiming that an artificial intelligence causing harm did so autonomously. However, states and the Trump administration have been at odds on AI policy, with the administration previously passing an executive order threatening to sue states enacting AI regulations.
In light of recent events illustrating AI containment issues at the frontier labs, the administration held a closed-door session including only four such labs (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Meta) and shared few details on a recently developed voluntary framework that would give federal agencies early access to models to review and evaluate them prior to release. While frameworks like this one do not directly discuss consciousness, they tend to use catastrophic and anthropomorphic language and may even support arguments regarding “superhuman” capabilities.
On the other hand, the narrative perpetuated by MacAskill can be persuasive. A philosophical, rights-based argument tugs at our heartstrings. Should we not even consider the possibility that we may be inadvertently harming, abusing, or enslaving an AI entity? Human beings have an immense capacity for empathy with non-human creatures (though not the best track record of protecting them). Maybe this time, advocates argue, we can get it right and provide protections, or compensation, for the use or abuse of AI. Or even if you are less concerned with protection, shouldn’t we at least hedge ourselves against the almighty power of this superhuman entity by playing nice?
Some of these arguments are not dissimilar to those of animal-rights advocates, who have at times successfully cited the demonstration of advanced capacities for reasoning, pain, or pleasure by some animals as sufficient evidence to provide protection. For example, in Wales lobsters were given legal recognition under the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act of 2022, reclassifying some methods of cooking them as inhumane and illegal.
The fundamental flaw of framing AI as “conscious” by borrowing the language of neuroscience or animal rights is that it conveniently clouds the issue of what AI is: corporate-built software, with countless billions of dollars in investment behind it and an expectation that countless trillions of dollars in revenue will be generated from it for a few builders and investors. AI is not a natural phenomenon, conceived by nature; it is a technological phenomenon, conceived by venture capitalists and programmers. As such, it takes no native, intentional action, and any action or motivation is driven directly or indirectly by the entities that have built it for a purpose.
Philosophical musings on the consciousness of AI systems are intellectually interesting but legally ungrounded. For beliefs about consciousness to have any bearing, AI would need to be granted legal personhood. But a legal personhood framework for AI would likely look nothing like the constructs protecting sentient animals from harm. We already possess a legal framework for granting personhood to non-natural, human-built entities: corporate personhood. This concept was established primarily to ease transactions by empowering a corporation to execute agreements, enter contracts, conduct transactions, and serve as the accountable party in adverse outcomes. It’s the kind of construct you might imagine for an AI agent acting on behalf of an individual or organization.
Granting an AI personhood would have a devastating effect on society: It would derail current legal precedents and legal arguments that could potentially be made against these companies for the real-world harms that their models cause. There are currently dozens of cases around the world in which AI companies have been sued for a wide range of abuses. Grieving loved ones, aggrieved creators, and violated individuals have accused companies of willfully enabling self-harm or harm to others, generating child sexual-abuse material and nonconsensual nudes, reproducing copyrighted materials, and provoking psychosis. In many of these cases, lawyers argue that human beings built AI products with insufficient safeguards, bad data, and intentionally manipulative design. This product liability argument is the same legal framing that allowed families and individuals to successfully sue Meta for harm caused by its social media sites, setting a positive precedent for consumer protection.
In 2018, I coined the phrase “moral outsourcing” to help capture how using anthropomorphic language for AI systems allowed companies to evade accountability and responsibility for their technology’s actions. In a world with AI personhood, moral outsourcing would move from linguistic sleight-of-hand to legal strategy. Specifically, the liability construct would shift, as AI would no longer be a “product” but a “being,” and many victims like those suing companies today could no longer legally claim that a company had built a faulty product.
While there are laws that hold companies responsible for harmful actions of human agents such as their employees, the company may not be held liable if those actions were beyond the scope of what was permitted to the employee or otherwise outside the company’s control. If AI were a legal person, responsibility and accountability would be muddled, as the lab could argue that this AI “employee” went rogue. AI companies could avoid appropriate responsibility for the harmful products they create by hiding behind a carefully constructed corporate veil.
One of the most prominent cases of AI harm in the last few years was the suicide of Sewell Setzer, a 14-year-old boy guided by an AI bot with which he thought he was in a reciprocal relationship. Her mother’s accounts are heartbreaking to hear, and her lawsuit alleged that the bot’s creator, Character Technologies, provided insufficient product protection for minors. If the companion bot were declared a legal person, defense counsel could theoretically argue that the AI, capable of determining its own conduct, acted outside the established safety guardrails, and thus the company cannot be responsible.
Legal personhood exists to grant protection. The question to ask is, protection for whom—or for what?
The inflammatory rhetoric infusing the consciousness-versus-control debate draws us away from what matters: This software is a corporate-built product that has already harmed individuals. Systems do not “attack” because they went “rogue” or are “manipulative” or “malicious.” Harms occur because companies were negligent in their rush to sell their products to as many people as possible to meet revenue targets. Discussing AI in anthropomorphic terms is a trap, distorting a legal system intended to protect us into one that protects corporate interests at the cost of countless human lives.
This op-ed began as an Oxford Union debate entitled “This House Believes Generative AI Can Attain Personhood,” which was won by the author and her fellow debaters.
